title: How To Keep the Spark of Improvement Aflame for the Students of Kentucky Kentucky-focused publication, September 1, 2026
author: B. Geoghegan
source: B. Geoghegan's Substack (bgeoghegan4.substack.com), originally printed in a
summary: Geoghegan surveys early signs that Kentucky's reading and math scores are recovering after pandemic-era declines, crediting the state's LETRS training of over 8,000 K-5 teachers in the science of reading and a 2024 law emphasizing foundational math skills. But the piece argues these gains coexist with deeper structural problems: a 93.5 percent graduation rate that masks the fact that over half of students aren't proficient in reading or math, and a state government that has resisted expanding school choice even as it protects homeschooling rights. The author points to Mississippi's reading-instruction turnaround, Texas's shift to sequential content-focused standards, and Louisiana's 'Let Teachers Teach' discipline initiative as models Kentucky could adopt without needing to reinvent anything, framing the state's task as replication and honest measurement rather than innovation.
points: Schools with higher concentrations of LETRS-trained teachers saw a 4.26 percent increase in reading proficiency from 2023 to 2025, tying the state's literacy gains directly to science-of-reading professional development.

The high graduation rate (93.5 percent, the nation's best) is reframed as a red flag rather than a success, since over half of students at all levels are not proficient in reading and even more are not proficient in math.

Mississippi jumped from 49th to 9th nationally in reading between 2013 and 2024 using evidence-informed instruction covering vocabulary, language acquisition, comprehension, and background knowledge — offered as Kentucky's clearest available model.

Louisiana's teacher-created 'Let Teachers Teach' initiative removed obstacles to effective instruction and improved both learning and teacher retention, addressing the argument that curriculum reform is wasted if classroom behavior expectations stay low.
Kentucky remains one of only 17 states with no private school choice program, which the author frames as leaving families whose public schools are failing their children with limited alternatives.
quotes: According to the Education Scorecard report, “Kentucky ranked 8th out of 38 states in academic growth in math and 5th out of 35 states in reading between 2022 and 2025.

The schools with higher concentrations of trained teachers saw a 4.26% increase from 2023 to 2025 in students reaching reading proficiency. The focus and investment on early literacy instruction that aligns with the cognitive science behind how students learn appears to be paying dividends for Kentucky’s youngest students.

While having the highest cohort graduation rate in the country at 93.5% seems worthy of applause, it is actually cause for concern when considering that over half of all elementary, middle, and high school students are not proficient in reading, with even larger percentages of students at all levels not proficient in math.

Kentucky can look to states like Mississippi, which has made remarkable gains. By using evidence-informed reading instruction that includes vocabulary, language acquisition, reading comprehension, and background knowledge, they jumped from 49th in 2013 to 9th in 2024, according to national assessments.
Their Let Teachers Teach initiative was created by teachers to remove obstacles to effective instruction. This initiative has improved student learning and teacher retention since its inception.
